boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Summit Point record (August 21, 1864) in Sheridan's Valley Campaign [August-October 1864]. The August 22 withdrawal to Halltown and the August 22-24 skirmishing there are context. Campaign-wide marches, destruction, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Divisions; the live field reads zero. Pond says Anderson brought Kershaw's division, Cutshaw's artillery and two cavalry brigades under Fitz Lee, and that Early advanced Rodes's and Ramseur's divisions against the Sixth Corps. Sheridan's August 22 dispatch says prisoners reported the whole enemy present with Longstreet, which he did not believe, one of Longstreet's divisions being there. His 1866 report gives about 18,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry effective on August 13.
claims.rationale: Unit identifications and a figure from eight days earlier; no count for either side on August 21. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Inconclusive and the live result Indecisive. Sheridan says the Sixth Corps' picket-line fight went very much in its favour and that the army moved back to Halltown without loss; Pond says the lost position was regained at nightfall and Anderson's advance was retarded by the cavalry at Berryville and Summit Point. NPS calls the Union actions effective delaying actions.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

open_questions: Wright's, Getty's, Merritt's and Wilson's reports, Hotchkiss's journal and the Confederate division reports remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office and field despatches; it quotes Sheridan's, Torbert's, Wright's and Early's reports and despatches and is not independent of them. Sheridan's dispatches of August-September 1864 and his report dated New Orleans, February 3, 1866 are one family of interested Union accounts. Official Records Series I, Volume XLIII, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
